item.title: 36 Bangladeshis among 96 detained at Bosnia border
item.description:
Ninety-six people, including 36 Bangladeshis, have been detained by border police in Bosnia and Herzegovina for allegedly attempting to illegally cross the country’s border.
The Gradiska Border Police, with assistance from the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, foiled two attempts to illegally cross the border on Wednesday, according to reports published Thursday by Sarajevo Times and First Balkan Media.
According to the Bosnia and Herzegovina Border Police, the first attempt involved 63 people and was stopped in Bistrica on Wednesday afternoon. The group included 40 Pakistani nationals and 23 Bangladeshis.
Acting on instructions from the prosecutor on duty at the Prosecutor’s Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina, authorities seized two boats at the scene and identified two people suspected of involvement in human trafficking.
Later that night, another attempt involving 33 people was foiled in Bistrica. The group included 13 Bangladeshis, 18 Afghans and two Pakistanis.
Authorities said the Banja Luka Field Centre of the Service for Foreigners’ Affairs had been informed of the incidents and that legal proceedings were underway.

item.title: Dhaka airport import cargo without scanner for 10 months
item.description:
The import cargo facility at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport has been without a scanner for the past 10 months, forcing Customs officials to rely on bills of entry and physical inspections to assess imported goods.
The absence of the scanner has raised concerns over the ability to detect illicit goods being brought into the country under the cover of legitimate consignments.
The issue came into focus after customs authorities recently seized 16kg of gold concealed inside fruit cartons from the airport’s import cargo facility.
The seizure was made based on prior intelligence, with customs officials later searching the consignment and recovering the gold.
Dhaka Customs House Commissioner Mashiur Rahman disclosed the information at a press conference held Thursday afternoon following the seizure of 20kg of gold at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
He said the scanner at the import cargo facility was damaged in a fire on October 18 last year and has not been replaced since.
“The process of purchasing a scanner is underway,” he said.
According to sources, customs officials seized 16kg of gold specially concealed inside fruit cartons from the import cargo facility on July 19.
Later, information emerged that another 10 consignments from the same company had arrived at the airport.
Those concerned said there was no way to guarantee that gold or other illicit goods had not been smuggled through those consignments.
They said Customs officials currently examine bills of entry and physically inspect imported goods. However, given the volume of cargo handled at the facility, it is not always possible to thoroughly inspect every item in large consignments.
As a result, large quantities of goods could potentially leave the facility without adequate examination, they said.
“This is a major threat for us,” they added.
Khairul Kabir Bhuiyan Mithu, vice-president of the C&F Agents Association, said having a scanner at the import cargo facility was essential.
“We have been hearing for several months that a scanner is coming. But it has not arrived yet,” he said.
Meanwhile, Customs Additional Commissioner Kamrul Islam said it was incorrect to suggest that goods were leaving the facility without inspection because there was no scanner.
“Our officials physically check every consignment,” he said.
However, having a scanner would make the inspection process easier, he added.
Scanner damaged in airport fire
A fire broke out at the Cargo Village Complex of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at noon on October 18 last year.
Thirty-seven units from 13 fire stations worked for nearly six and a half hours to bring the blaze under control.
Goods worth hundreds of crores of taka were destroyed in the fire.
The scanner at the import cargo facility was also damaged in the incident and has remained out of operation since then.

item.title: ChatGPT hit by widespread outage as reports surge past 43,000
item.description:
ChatGPT suffered a widespread disruption on Thursday, with tens of thousands of users reporting problems accessing or using the AI platform as OpenAI investigated issues affecting ChatGPT and Codex.
Reports on outage-tracking service Downdetector rose rapidly, from more than 5,000 shortly before 9pm Bangladesh time to over 22,000 within minutes and then past 43,000, indicating a sharp escalation in the disruption.
OpenAI initially showed no problems on its official status page before acknowledging that it was investigating issues affecting ChatGPT and Codex.
The company had not immediately disclosed the cause.
The disruption came after several service problems in recent days.
Earlier Thursday, OpenAI reported high error rates affecting ChatGPT Work Mode.
That incident began at 6:04am Bangladesh time and was resolved six minutes later.
On Wednesday, the company resolved errors preventing some users from creating new accounts, while ChatGPT Work also experienced elevated errors and latency earlier in the week.
OpenAI notes that its availability figures are aggregated across subscription tiers, models and error types, meaning individual users may encounter problems even when its overall status appears normal.
The scale of Thursday’s user reports made the latest disruption potentially one of the more significant ChatGPT service interruptions in recent days, although the full extent and cause remained unclear.

item.title: TIB: Hopes for independent NHRC remain unfulfilled
item.description:
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) has said that proposed laws on the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) and enforced disappearances still fail to ensure independent, impartial and conflict-free investigations into serious human rights violations.
The anti-graft watchdog said several positive amendments were proposed by the parliamentary standing committee during its review of the National Human Rights Commission Bill, 2026 and the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, 2026.
However, it said fundamental weaknesses remain, particularly regarding the NHRC’s ability to independently investigate allegations against law enforcement agencies on its own initiative.
Against the backdrop of Bangladesh’s experience of prolonged and serious human rights violations, TIB called for meaningful parliamentary discussion on every important provision of the two bills before their passage, with participation from both government and opposition lawmakers.
TIB welcomed several recommendations made by the parliamentary committee on the NHRC bill, including mandatory representation of indigenous or disadvantaged communities, disqualification of loan defaulters from becoming commissioners, and removal of the requirement for prior approval to visit detention centres other than military detention centres.
However, TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman said the proposed law still does not provide sufficient safeguards for an independent commission.
“The absence of a clear provision that the Commission shall not fall under any ministry or division of the government; the scope for a serving government employee to become a commissioner while on deputation, lien or unpaid leave; the risk of unchecked executive influence through the composition of the selection committee; the deputation of up to 30% of the Commission’s total staff from government service; and the failure to guarantee full financial independence together mean that hopes for a genuinely independent Human Rights Commission remain unfulfilled,” he said.
He said the proposed structure could result in a commission being established without ensuring its independence.
“In other words, a commission is being formed, but the hope that it will be independent remains an illusion,” he said.
Dr Iftekharuzzaman also questioned provisions under which the commission would have to seek reports from the relevant force or institution instead of conducting its own investigation into serious human rights violations by disciplinary forces.
He said the proposed arrangement effectively leaves investigative authority in the hands of institutions accused of violations.
TIB also expressed concern that military detention centres have been excluded from the places that the National Preventive Mechanism unit may inspect regularly and without prior notice.
The organisation said the proposed bill has also narrowed several important functions of the commission, including providing legal assistance to aggrieved persons, conducting human rights training, examining the consistency of laws with international human rights instruments, and undertaking other activities necessary to promote and protect human rights.
Regarding the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, TIB said the parliamentary committee had not recommended any fundamental change to the core investigative framework.
The organisation described the proposed amendments as largely “cosmetic” in terms of ensuring independent investigations, accountability and victims’ rights.
Dr Iftekharuzzaman said Section 19 of the NHRC bill retains the arrangement under which the commission would seek a report from the concerned force or institution in cases involving serious human rights violations by disciplinary forces.
“By narrowing the Commission’s power of inquiry and investigation and making it dependent on reports, this provision makes it weaker than even the 2009 law and inconsistent with the Paris Principles,” he said.
He said the enforced disappearance bill has a similar weakness.
Although Section 14(3) bars an accused force from investigating its own members, the provision allows responsibility to be assigned to another disciplinary force or an inter-force investigation team.
TIB questioned whether such an arrangement could ensure genuine independence when members of various disciplinary, police, intelligence and security agencies have been accused of involvement in past enforced disappearance cases.
“Is the investigating institution genuinely independent from that same justice-obstructing institutional circle, or is it being asked to investigate itself?” Dr Iftekharuzzaman asked.
He warned that a weak or biased investigation could obstruct justice and deprive victims and their families of recognition, compensation and rights relating to the use and inheritance of property.
TIB also called for a more comprehensive definition of enforced disappearance in line with the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance (ICPPED).
Dr Iftekharuzzaman said the definition should explicitly cover possible involvement by public representatives, MPs, ministers, advisers and other influential state actors, alongside government employees and members of disciplinary forces.
He also raised concerns over Section 15, saying it was unclear how an accused senior official could be shielded from proceedings based on an interim report prepared by a subordinate investigator without the process being vulnerable to influence.
He said this could create a risk of impunity for accused officials.
TIB further pointed out that Section 16 does not retain safeguards included in the 2025 ordinance requiring searches to continue until a disappeared person is found or their fate is established and requiring families to be regularly informed of progress.
The organisation also said penalties for some offences have been reduced compared with the 2025 ordinance.
While the minimum sentence for enforced disappearance remains three years, the bill provides for a maximum of five years’ rigorous imprisonment for false or harassing accusations.
Dr Iftekharuzzaman warned that such a provision could discourage families from filing complaints if the investigation process itself is vulnerable to conflicts of interest and institutional influence.
“When the investigation mechanism itself carries the risk of conflict of interest and institutional influence, there is a real concern that, for want of adequate evidence, the failure to prove a genuine allegation could instead be blamed on the complainant’s family,” he said.
“Such a provision risks creating a serious culture of fear among victims when it comes to lodging complaints and seeking justice.”
TIB said it had shared its observations on the NHRC law from the drafting stage and, following Cabinet approval, submitted 25 recommendations on the NHRC bill and 17 recommendations on the Enforced Disappearance Prevention Bill.
Dr Iftekharuzzaman said the parliamentary review provided an opportunity to address the fundamental weaknesses in the two bills, but several core concerns raised by stakeholders remain unresolved.
“We expect that, instead of being passed hastily by voice vote, the bills will be amended following meaningful discussion in Parliament on every important provision and proposed amendment, with all members rising above partisan loyalty and guided by their moral and humane values,” he said.
He warned that if the 13th Parliament passes the bills without the necessary amendments to bring them in line with the Paris Principles, ICPPED and other international standards, it would fail to meet public expectations for human rights protection.
The call comes amid broader concerns from rights groups that the proposed framework leaves investigations into enforced disappearance with the police rather than establishing an independent investigative mechanism.

item.title: State Minister Shama urges investment in cosmetics industry
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has called for greater local and foreign investment in Bangladesh’s cosmetics, skincare and personal care industry, saying the sector has the potential to become a major manufacturing and export hub.
She made the remarks while inaugurating Cosmética Dhaka 2026 at the International Convention City Bashundhara (ICCB) in Dhaka on Thursday.
Speaking as the chief guest, Shama Obaed said Bangladesh could leverage the production capacity, compliance infrastructure, skilled workforce and global buyer networks developed through its readymade garment industry to build a competitive cosmetics sector.
“By leveraging the production capacity, compliance infrastructure, skilled workforce and global buyer relationships that we have developed in the readymade garment industry, it is possible to establish contract manufacturing, formulation, specialized packaging, quality laboratories and certification facilities in the cosmetics sector as well,” she said.
She also highlighted the potential of Bangladesh’s agricultural and natural resources.
“If we can build a strong supply chain of certified botanical and herbal ingredients by utilizing Bangladesh’s agriculture and natural resources, this sector will not only meet domestic demand but also open new export opportunities for Bangladesh in the global market,” she said.
The state minister said the government wanted to take the industry beyond “Made in Bangladesh” towards “Formulated, Developed and Branded in Bangladesh”.
She called for investment facilitation, internationally recognized testing and certification, intellectual property protection, sustainable packaging and support for small and medium-sized entrepreneurs.
“If we can establish an integrated industrial base by ensuring environmentally friendly production, safe raw materials and international standards, the cosmetics and personal care sector could emerge as a new and powerful area for foreign currency earnings, employment generation and economic diplomacy in Bangladesh,” she added.
Cosmética Dhaka 2026 features brands, manufacturers, suppliers, retailers and health experts from 16 countries, including South Korea, Thailand, the United States, France, Singapore, China, Japan and India.
The three-day exhibition has more than 100 stalls, along with live demonstrations, beauty consultations, expert discussions and networking opportunities.
BIAA President Baharul Monsur said the cosmetics and personal care industry had been growing every year and called for more investment through the exhibition.
Frank Kenton, senior perfumer at Senses International Ltd, said Bangladesh was one of the promising markets in South Asia, but products must remain affordable for consumers.
SM Faisal Munim, CEO of Squad Mind Global Ltd, said the organizers expected the exhibition to attract more local and foreign investment and establish itself as a business-matching platform.
The exhibition will remain open to visitors from 10am to 7pm every day.

item.title: Thirty injured as picnic bus collides head-on with passenger bus in Natore
item.description:
At least 30 teachers, students and guardians of Shaheen School’s Sirajganj branch were injured when a bus carrying them collided head-on with a passenger bus in Baraigram upazila of Natore on Thursday.
The accident occurred around 10am in the Manikpur area of the Bonpara-Hatikumrul highway as the school group was travelling to Safina Park in Rajshahi for an annual picnic.
The collision left the front sections of both buses badly damaged. Traffic on the highway remained halted for about an hour before the vehicles were removed and movement resumed, reports Bangla Tribune.
According to eyewitness Hossain Ali, the school bus was heading towards Rajshahi when it collided head-on with a Dhaka-bound passenger bus in Manikpur. No one was killed, but at least 30 people travelling on the picnic bus were injured.
The injured include Rezaul Karim, 39; Zainal Abedin, 26; Sinha Islam, 7; Sonali Khatun, 25; Barsha Khatun, 20; Taslim Ahmed, 33; Hazrat Ali, 50; Dighi Khatun, 12; Rabbi Hasan, 24; Ashraful Islam, 42; Beauty Begum, 26; Hawa Begum, 30; Monirul Islam, 33; Habiba Khatun, 12; another Rezaul Karim, 45; Kabya Hossain, 12; and Mostafizur Rahman, 46.
Fire Service personnel from Bonpara, highway police and local residents rescued the injured and took them to Baraigram Upazila Health Complex and Amina Hospital in Bonpara for treatment.
Five teachers of Shaheen School alleged that the passenger bus was travelling recklessly at high speed and suddenly rammed into their bus. Some passengers fell from their seats while others were thrown against the windows, causing panic inside the bus.
The driver of the passenger bus fled the scene following the crash, they said.
The school’s picnic programme has been cancelled following the accident. The injured are being taken back to Sirajganj after receiving treatment.
SI Alamgir Hossain of Bonpara Highway Police Station said the two buses involved in the accident had been seized.

item.title: Ziaur Rahman Medical College interns call off strike
item.description:
Intern doctors at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College (SHZMC) Hospital in Bogra called off their two-day strike on Thursday after authorities assured them of increased security and action against those accused of attacking doctors.
The interns began the strike at midnight on Tuesday after several colleagues were injured when relatives of a patient who died at the hospital allegedly attacked doctors on duty.
They decided to resume work following a nearly three-hour meeting involving political leaders, the district administration and hospital authorities at the hospital auditorium on Thursday.
Intern doctor Ritul Mondal Snigdha confirmed the decision.
SHZMC Hospital Deputy Director Dr Manzur-e-Morshed said the meeting was held in a cordial atmosphere and the interns agreed to return to work after being assured that their demands would be addressed.
Their demands included expelling those involved in the attack who allegedly acted in the name of the Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD), increasing police presence, deploying armed Ansar personnel and appointing the required staff for 18 beds.
The interns resumed their normal duties from Thursday night, the deputy director said.
Meanwhile, five JCD leaders were expelled from the organization over their alleged involvement in the incident.
Abdul Malek, of Rajapur village in Bogra Sadar, died while undergoing treatment in the Medicine Ward on the seventh floor of the hospital at around 10pm on Tuesday.
Following his death, his relatives allegedly attacked doctors on duty with locally made weapons. Several doctors were injured, including intern doctor Mohammad Ali Jinnah, who suffered a broken hand, and Azraf Islam, who sustained bleeding injuries.
At a press briefing on Wednesday, the interns said at least 15 of their colleagues had been injured, six of them seriously.
The attackers also allegedly vandalized medical equipment and government property, causing an estimated Tk2.1 lakh in damage. Three mobile phones and a stethoscope were reportedly taken from the ward.
Police rushed to the hospital and brought the situation under control.
Hospital Ward Master Anwar Hossain filed a case with Bogra Sadar police station, naming seven people and eight to 10 unidentified individuals as accused.
Police arrested six people on Wednesday afternoon and, following a court order, sent them to Bogra jail.
While Thursday’s meeting was underway, Bogra city JCD announced the expulsion of five leaders for disciplinary violations.
They are Ward 18 Convener Nafiul Islam, Senior Joint Convener Monir Hossain, Joint Convener Md Pranto Islam, member Rakibul Hasan Rakib and Ward 19 Assistant Organizational Secretary SM Shihab.
District JCD President Habibur Rashid Sandhan said strict organizational and legal action was being taken against those involved in the attack.
The interns’ strike disrupted services at the hospital for two days, although emergency services remained operational. Patients and their relatives travelling from different areas faced difficulties.
At around 10am on Thursday, the interns also closed the outpatient department ticket counter, causing anger among patients and their relatives. The counter reopened after hospital authorities intervened.
During Thursday’s meeting, District Commissioner Toufikur Rahman, Police Superintendent Mirza Sayem Mahmud, District Council Administrator AKM Ahsanul Tayeb Zakir, Bogra City Corporation Administrator MR Islam Swadhin, former SHZMC principal Professor Dr Moudud Hossain Alamgir Pavel, current principal Professor Dr Wadudul Haque Tarafdar, Deputy Director Dr Manzur-e-Morshed, medical leaders, and social and political leaders were present.
Hospital services returned to normal after the interns called off their strike.

item.title: Myanmar vows ‘safe’ returns ahead of Malaysia repatriations
item.description:
Myanmar pledged on Thursday “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after the United Nations and rights groups raised concerns about the upcoming repatriation of 1,500 people from Malaysia.
The Myanmar foreign ministry also repeated its disavowal of the persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority, members of which campaigners fear may be plunged back into danger by the return scheme.
In July, Malaysia said Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of the Rohingya, a group which has faced a campaign of violent discrimination in Myanmar since 2017.
Both countries say a first wave of nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals will be repatriated voluntarily in late September, although it is unclear how many Rohingya will be included.
“Myanmar is committed to working closely with Bangladesh and friendly countries to facilitate the voluntary return of verified displaced persons in a safe and dignified manner,” the foreign ministry statement said.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled Myanmar after a brutal military crackdown starting in 2017, which is the basis of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
More than 1.2 million live just over the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, but talk of repatriations has yielded little progress.
Another 126,000 Rohingya live in Malaysia, alongside displaced Myanmar citizens from different ethnic groups.
Myanmar has long denied the Rohingya have a distinct heritage, saying they are descendants of immigrants from Bangladesh -- even refusing to use the term “Rohingya.”
The foreign ministry repeated its assertion on Thursday that the term “falsely claims an ethnic identity which has never existed in Myanmar,” as it condemned recent commemorations in some countries for Rohingya Genocide Remembrance Day.
Malaysia’s communications minister Fahmi Fadzil has said his country will not repatriate Myanmar nationals “if they would either be persecuted or their lives would be threatened.”
But rights monitors fear returning the Rohingya to a country where their identities are erased will permit a new wave of abuses.
A report by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres published Wednesday found “conditions for their voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable return do not currently exist.”
Many migrants in Malaysia are also being held in detention centers, raising questions about whether their decisions to return can be freely made.

item.title: 429 arrested, weapons recovered in DMP raids over 24 hours
item.description:
A total of 429 people were arrested in regular raids conducted by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) across the capital over the past 24 hours.
During the operations, police also recovered several illegal firearms, 822 yaba pills, 19kg 185g of cannabis and 88 bottles of Eskaf syrup. A total of 64 cases were filed during the period.
Deputy Commissioner of the DMP’s Media and Public Relations Division Md Akter Hossain confirmed the information on Thursday.
Four people were arrested in connection with a gunfight in Gandaria, and a foreign-made pistol and yaba were recovered following the incident.
In a separate operation in Banani, five people were arrested with a foreign-made pistol while allegedly preparing to commit a robbery.
In Mirpur, notorious criminal and shooter Zakir was arrested with firearms and ammunition.
Meanwhile, the DMP’s City Intelligence Analysis Division arrested a suspected drug dealer and recovered 7kg of cannabis.
Of the 429 arrested, 22 were detained by the Ramna Division, 22 by the Lalbagh Division, 39 by the Wari Division, 66 by the Motijheel Division, 62 by the Tejgaon Division, 144 by the Mirpur Division, 35 by the Gulshan Division, 39 by the Uttara Division and two by the Detective Branch.
The arrests were made during operations in various police station areas across the capital, where police also recovered other evidence and narcotics.
Legal proceedings against the arrested individuals are underway, the DMP said.

item.title: Madrasa student death: Father protests teacher’s bail, questions suicide theory
item.description:
The father of an eight-year-old madrasa student found hanging in a teachers’ toilet in Jatrabari on Thursday questioned how his son could have died by suicide as a Dhaka court granted bail to one of three teachers accused in the case.
“An eight-year-old child cannot commit suicide. My son could not even tie a mosquito-net rope. How could he hang himself?” Ziaur Rahman said after the court granted bail to Hafez Mohammad Ullah.
He also questioned how the knot around his son’s neck had been tied, saying even a sensible person could not have made such a knot.
Ziaur Rahman was present at the court to oppose Mohammad Ullah’s bail and expressed frustration over the order, as well as the fact that the other two accused teachers have not been arrested.
“They are moving around openly. The law enforcement agencies are not arresting them,” he said.
Dhaka’s 15th Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge Mizanur Rahman granted Mohammad Ullah bail after hearing arguments from both sides.
SM Abul Kalam (Azad), lawyer for the complainant, confirmed the matter.
The court granted Mohammad Ullah bail on a Tk1,000 bond until the police report is submitted.
Mohammad Ullah was arrested nearly two months after the case was filed and has remained in jail since then.
During the hearing, his lawyer, Abul Kalam Khan, sought bail, saying his client was not involved in the incident and had been implicated in the case as part of a conspiracy.
He said Mohammad Ullah was the sole earning member of his family and that his detention had left his family struggling.
“Any condition may be imposed for his bail,” the lawyer said.
Opposing the bail, Alhaz Borhan Uddin, chief prosecutor in the BDR mutiny case, said CCTV footage from the madrasa showed the child appearing cheerful and energetic on the afternoon of the incident.
He said it was suspicious that the eight-year-old was later found dead in the teachers’ toilet with a gamcha, a traditional thin cotton towel, around his neck.
“The accused killed the child. We oppose his bail,” he said.
Child found dead in teachers’ toilet

The child was found with a gamcha wrapped around his neck.
The following day, his father filed a murder case against three teachers — Maulana Qari Anisur Rahman, teacher-in-charge Hafez Maulana Zahirul Islam and Hafez Mohammad Ullah.
According to the case statement, Ziaur Rahman suspects that the accused may have attempted to sexually assault his son or that the child may have witnessed an incident involving them.
He alleged that the three accused, along with four or five unidentified people, killed Mudachchir sometime between 4:15pm and 6:30pm on December 20.
He further alleged that the body was hung from the ventilation of the teachers’ toilet with a gamcha to divert the investigation.
The other two accused have yet to be arrested, according to the father.

item.title: Court orders seizure of ex-railway minister’s 18 plots, 2 cars
item.description:
A Dhaka court has ordered the seizure of 18 plots of land in Comilla, along with two Toyota vehicles owned by former railway minister Md Mujibul Haque, in a corruption case. The court also ordered the freezing of six bank accounts held in his name.
Dhaka Metropolitan Senior Special Judge Md Shahjahan Kabir passed the order on Thursday following an application by Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Assistant Director Papon Kumar Saha.
According to the ACC, Mujibul Haque allegedly abused his power while serving as a public servant, including as railway minister and lawmaker, and, in collusion with others, acquired and possessed Tk7.39 crore in assets beyond his known sources of income through dishonest means.
The ACC filed the case against him under Section 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
During the investigation, scrutiny of records found that attempts were being made to transfer or dispose of movable and immovable assets owned by or linked to the accused, the ACC said in its application.
The commission said transferring or disposing of the assets before the case is resolved could cause significant financial loss, prompting it to seek the court’s order to secure the properties.

item.title: Andaleeve: Govt won't interfere in media’s work
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Andaleeve Rahman has said the government will not interfere in the work of the media and wants journalists to work independently.
“The media is one of the pillars of democracy. The government will not interfere in the work of the media in any way,” he said.
Andaleeve made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at an exchange meeting with local journalists at the Bhola Press Club auditorium around 11:30am on Thursday.
He said the government would take necessary initiatives regarding journalists’ demands related to the Wage Board, welfare, training and media policies.
“You will judge whether our work is being done well or badly. However, journalists’ pens should not unnecessarily harm anyone’s reputation,” he said.
The minister said he had never called any journalist to prevent the publication of a report or interfered in the politics of any press club during his nearly two decades in politics.
“I was never interested in having 10 journalists write in my favour or calling them and destroying their jobs if they did not. We want to move away from this practice,” he said.
He urged journalists to scrutinize the government’s activities and point out its mistakes and shortcomings.
“You will work independently in your own way. You will criticise the government’s work and point out its mistakes and shortcomings,” Andaleeve said.
“However, reports should not be driven by hatred, half-truths or fabrication. A wrong report can destroy a person’s life, career and reputation.”
The minister also expressed concern over the growing prevalence of cyberbullying, saying it was affecting public trust in the media.
“People now sometimes see genuine news and consider it fake news. As a result, the media is also facing questions,” he said.
Referring to journalists’ demands, Andaleeve invited a small delegation of local journalists to Dhaka for discussions.
“We will discuss what you want and which issues require policy decisions. I will speak to the prime minister and try to implement what is possible,” he said.
Chairing the meeting, Bhola Press Club President Nazrul Haque called for the speedy implementation of the Wage Board, a modern journalistic policy, regular district-level training through the Press Institute of Bangladesh (PIB), and effective initiatives for journalists’ welfare.
He also sought the Information Ministry’s assistance in renovating and developing the press club building.
Press Club General Secretary Nasir Uddin Liton and Cultural Secretary Mashiur Rahman moderated the meeting.

item.title: Injured tea worker leader arrested over Tk500 wage protest
item.description:
A tea worker leader, who was allegedly injured in an attack during a protest demanding a daily wage of Tk500, has been arrested and sent to jail after being named the prime accused in a case filed over the incident in Srimangal, Moulvibazar.
Gita Rani Kanu, one of the key leaders of the movement, was detained by police on Wednesday night and later sent to jail by a Moulvibazar court.
The protesters alleged that the case was deliberately filed against them while they were receiving treatment for injuries sustained in the alleged attack.
The clash occurred on Monday during a human chain and rally in the Choumuhana area. Protesters alleged that leaders of the Bangladesh Tea Workers' Union attacked them, leaving 10 to 12 workers injured. Several of the injured received treatment at Moulvibazar Sadar Hospital.
Srimangal Police Station Officer-in-Charge Abdullah Al Mamun said a case had been filed naming Gita Rani Kanu as the prime accused, along with four other named individuals and six to seven unidentified persons.
According to the case, Bangladesh Tea Workers' Union Central Committee General Secretary Nipen Pal filed the complaint under several sections of the Penal Code, including those relating to unlawful assembly, assault, vandalism, theft and criminal intimidation.
The other named accused are Janak Lal Deshwara, Akash Goala, Bishwo Prasad Goala and Gopal Yadav.
The case alleges that the accused entered the Labour House as a group, assaulted Nipen Pal, stole Tk5,700 in cash and vandalised furniture, causing an estimated Tk20,000 in damage. Before her arrest, Gita Rani Kanu said the protesters had planned to march towards the offices of the DDL and the Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) under their scheduled programme and had obtained police permission.
She alleged that they were attacked while passing the road in front of the tea workers' union office.
According to Gita, tea worker leader Dulal Hazra first tore their banner. She alleged that union treasurer Paresh Kalindi and leader Subash Ravidash then took several protesters near the gate of the union office, where General Secretary Nipen Pal, Balishira Valley President Bijoy Hazra, Suman Hazra, Suman Tati and others allegedly assaulted them.
Gita said she, Janak Lal Deshwara and Radha Mohan Nuniya received treatment at Moulvibazar Sadar Hospital following the incident.
She alleged that as they were undergoing treatment, they could not immediately file a case. When they later went to the police station, they learned that a case had instead been filed against them.
Another tea worker leader Akash Dosad claimed that video footage of the alleged attack was available. He alleged that the assault took place in the presence of police, who did not intervene to protect the protesters.
He further alleged that those responsible for the attack vandalised the union office themselves and were attempting to blame the protesters.
Union denies attack allegations Bangladesh Tea Workers' Union General Secretary Nipen Pal denied allegations that union leaders had attacked the protesters. He alleged that the protesters entered the union office, created disorder and used abusive language in an attempt to take control of the premises, prompting him to file the case. Asked whether any video footage or CCTV recordings were available to support allegations of vandalism inside the office, Nipen said there were no CCTV cameras on the premises. He denied personally assaulting anyone and said the alleged altercation should be investigated. Moulvibazar Sadar Hospital Residential Medical Officer Ahmed Faisal Zaman said three injured people were admitted to the hospital and discharged the following day after receiving treatment. One of the injured, Janak Lal, alleged that he later had to seek treatment elsewhere because of security concerns following the filing of the case. Tea workers have been continuing their movement, demanding a daily wage of Tk500, the withdrawal of a 5 percent increment, land rights and union elections, among other demands. Union leaders, however, said they were examining whether demands for an “interim committee”, raised during the programme, indicated an agenda beyond the wage movement.

item.title: Sailing boats stage comeback on Jamuna in Bogra
item.description:
Traditional sailing boats, once a familiar sight on the Jamuna River in Sariakandi of Bogra, have returned to the waterways as soaring fuel prices prompt local boatmen to revive the age-old mode of transport.
The boats are now mainly used to collect grass from river chars for cattle and goats and to carry light goods. Boatmen say they can save considerably on fuel costs by relying on wind power instead of engines.
The return of the colorful boats has also added to the scenic beauty of the Jamuna.
With varying winds currently blowing across the river, several sailing boats can be seen plying the water, especially in the morning.
The traditional boats generally have either square or triangular sails. Square-sailed boats use three bamboo poles, while triangular-sailed ones use two. A large bamboo pole is fixed vertically in the middle of the boat as a mast, with one or two additional poles attached to it. Thick, colorful cloth is then stretched across the poles to form the sail.
As wind fills the sail, the boat moves across the river. The boatman controls its direction by adjusting the sail with a rope.
Locals said sailing boats were common on the Jamuna, Bangali and other rivers in Sariakandi even in the 1990s. They gradually disappeared after engine-powered boats became widely available.
Traditional boats such as Bojra, Pansi and Mayurpankhi were once a striking feature of the region's waterways, known for their distinctive sails.
Dhalu Fakir, a resident of Sariakandi Sadar Union, said people once depended on sailing boats for long-distance travel and for transporting agricultural produce and other goods.
“Rows of sailing boats could be seen on the river in those days. They were beautiful to watch,” he said.
Fakir said he recently resumed using a sailing boat because of the sharp increase in fuel prices.
“I don't have to use an engine or spend money on diesel and other fuels. It saves me money,” he said.
He now crosses the Jamuna by sailboat every morning to reach a river char, where he cuts grass for his cattle and goats before sailing back home.
The experience, he said, also brings back memories of his childhood.
Sariakandi Upazila Nirbahi Officer S M Mikail Islam said some poor boatmen and livestock owners living along the Jamuna had resumed using traditional sailing boats to reduce fuel expenses.
“The boats are helping them save money while also reducing environmental pollution. At the same time, their return is adding to the beauty of the Jamuna,” he said.

item.title: SalamAir launches direct Sylhet-Muscat flights after eight-year
item.description:
Oman-based airline SalamAir has launched direct flights between Sylhet and Muscat, marking the return of a foreign airline to Sylhet MAG Osmani International Airport after an eight-year hiatus.
A SalamAir flight from Muscat landed at Osmani Airport at 7:30am on Tuesday, carrying 133 passengers. The return flight departed Sylhet at 8:45am. The inaugural flight was welcomed with a ceremonial water-cannon salute as it entered the airport’s taxiway, according to SalamAir Sylhet Area In-Charge Selim Al Razi.
SalamAir Chief Commercial Officer Steve Allen attended the inaugural ceremony as the chief guest, while Fatihah Ahmed Al Balushi, Deputy Chief of Mission at the Embassy of Oman, was present as the special guest.
Officials from the airport, Biman Bangladesh Airlines and SalamAir were also present at the ceremony. They included Sylhet Osmani International Airport Director Mohammad Hafiz Ahmed, Biman Sylhet District Manager Shariful Alam, SalamAir Bangladesh Country Manager Mohammad Rajon and SalamAir Area Manager Sajid Khan.
To mark the occasion, SalamAir distributed sweets among passengers arriving from and departing for Muscat. Guests were also welcomed with flowers before attending a luncheon hosted by the airline at a city restaurant.
Speaking at the event, Steve Allen said Sylhet and Muscat had longstanding social and economic ties, and the new direct service would further strengthen those connections.
SalamAir will initially operate three flights a week on the Sylhet-Muscat route. The frequency is expected to rise to five flights a week from October in response to growing demand. The airline also plans to introduce daily flights from January 2027, subject to necessary approvals.
The new service is also expected to reduce the cost of Umrah travel for passengers from Sylhet. Several travel agencies have already announced Umrah packages covering the Sylhet-Muscat-Jeddah route via SalamAir for around Tk1.2 lakh.
SalamAir currently operates 24 weekly flights from Bangladesh, including 14 from Chattogram, seven from Dhaka and three from Sylhet.
Dubai-based flydubai was the first foreign airline to operate from Osmani International Airport, launching its Sylhet-Dubai service in April 2015. However, the route was suspended in September 2018 due to operational reasons.
SalamAir’s new service therefore marks the return of foreign airline operations to Sylhet after nearly eight years.

item.title: Faridpur farmers worry over low jute prices despite bumper yields
item.description:
Jute farmers in Faridpur are expecting a good harvest this season, thanks to favourable weather and adequate water during the retting period, but rising production costs have left them worried about getting fair prices.
Faridpur is one of Bangladesh’s major jute-producing districts. This year, jute was cultivated on around 87,400 hectares of land, slightly above the target of 87,328 hectares set by the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE).
The DAE expects the district to produce around 196,000 tonnes of jute this season.
Farmers and traders said jute is currently selling for Tk 4,000 to Tk 4,200 per maund, depending on its variety and quality, at markets including Kanaipur, Naler Mor, Talma, Kadiradi, Satair and Barga.
At the current market rate, the total value of this season’s jute production in the district could exceed Tk 2,000 crore, according to the agriculture department.
Shahduzzaman, deputy director of the DAE in Faridpur, said weather conditions had been favourable throughout the season.
“The weather was quite favourable for jute production this year. Adequate water in canals and wetlands during the retting period helped ensure good colour and quality of the fibre,” he said.
He said the department expected around 196,000 tonnes of jute to be produced in the district this season.
Despite the good yield and quality, however, farmers said their production costs had increased significantly due to higher prices of fertiliser, seeds, labour and other agricultural inputs.
Saiful Islam, Nasir Hossain and Anwar Hossain, among several jute growers in Saltha, said they needed at least Tk 4,000 per maund to cover their costs.
The yield has been good, but the cost of fertiliser, seeds, labour and other inputs has gone up. Unless we get more than Tk 4,000 per maund, we will not make a profit. There is even a risk of losses, they said.
The farmers urged the authorities to take steps to ensure a fair price for jute in line with production costs and prevailing market conditions.
They said a fair price would encourage farmers to continue cultivating jute and help increase production of the country’s traditional cash crop.

item.title: Iran war is not a war, US VP Vance says
item.description:
USA-TRUMP/

US Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he would not categorise the Iran war as a war, despite continuing clashes with Tehran six months after the start of the conflict.

Vance's comments came amid growing signs that President Donald Trump is trying to draw a line under the conflict that has bogged down his administration.

"I wouldn't call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting," Vance told a White House briefing when asked if the war would be over by US midterm elections in November.

Vance added that "I recognise there have been places where this has flared up" but said major combat operations only lasted for six weeks after the US-Israel war started on 28 February.

Iran, US trade threats after fresh strikes

"But when you ask when will this end, you're asking me a question like when will the Iranians stop shooting at ships? I think the reality is I don't know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians," he said.

After several weeks of calm, fresh clashes began with US raids on Sunday, deepening the impasse in the six-month war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

Vance insisted that the United States would not reopen talks with Iran until it ended attacks on commercial shipping.

But with fuel prices threatening to cost Trump's Republicans their control of Congress at the ballot box, his administration has begun pushing the message that oil flows through the waterway are now returning to pre-war levels.

Wedding strike probe

"Their control over the Strait of Hormuz is effectively gone," Vance said of Iran.

"If you go back three months ago, how much oil and gas was coming out of the strait under Iranian threats? It was virtually nothing. Now, it's almost back to where it was before the conflict even started," Vance said.

Trump's approval ratings are near record lows as the president who vowed to keep the United States out of any more foreign wars finds himself in a quagmire with the Islamic republic.

Eighteen US troops and thousands of people in Iran and Lebanon have died in the conflict since February.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was now discussing with senior aides about whether to declare the Iran war over. He posted a photo of a banner saying "Mission Accomplished" last week.

US strike kills 5 and wounds dozens of civilians at a wedding, Iran says

Iran pressed on with fresh attacks on Thursday, saying it hit US military bases in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates to avenge a strike on a wedding that it blamed on Washington.

Vance said the United States was probing the wedding strike but cast doubt on Iranian reporting of the incident.

"I know that we're investigating," Vance said. "I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far. So I'm extremely skeptical of this."

The Iranian Red Crescent said the missile attack on the wedding in the Iranian coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people late Tuesday, including a child, and wounded more than 50.

item.title: Bangladeshis advised to book hotels before travelling to Kolkata
item.description:
Following a fire in Kolkata, India, on 19 August, the local administration has temporarily closed a number of residential hotels. As a result, Bangladeshis travelling there for medical treatment or other purposes may face difficulties finding accommodation.

To avoid such problems, the Bangladesh Deputy High Commission in Kolkata has advised Bangladeshi citizens not to travel there without securing a hotel booking in advance.

The Bangladesh Deputy High Commission in Kolkata issued the advisory in a notice today, Thursday.

According to the notice, following the tragic fire in Kolkata on 19 August, the local administration temporarily closed residential hotels and restaurants deemed prone to accidents as a precautionary measure.

Local authorities have said it could take more than a month for these hotels to reopen after complying with safety requirements and other regulations. In this situation, Bangladeshi citizens have been specifically requested not to travel to Kolkata without first confirming their hotel accommodation, in order to avoid difficulties in finding a place to stay.

The advisory asks travellers to confirm their hotel bookings before travelling and to make sure they are properly informed about the hotel’s current operations, room availability and location.

In addition, companions accompanying patients travelling to Kolkata for medical treatment must confirm their hotel bookings before arriving in the city. The notice also requests travellers to verify the availability of rooms at the relevant hotel, the validity of the booking, the distance between the hotel and the hospital, and other necessary facilities.

India unsure whether Tarique Rahman or his representative will attend BRICS
item.description:
The Indian government still does not know whether Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will attend the upcoming BRICS Summit or, if he does not, whether someone else will represent Bangladesh at the event.

Responding to a question on the matter at the Indian Ministry of External Affairs’ briefing on Friday, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said he had no new information on the issue.

India has invited Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to attend the outreach session of the BRICS Summit in his capacity as chair of BIMSTEC. The summit is scheduled to take place in New Delhi on 12 and 13 September.

India had earlier confirmed that the BRICS invitation was extended separately from an invitation for a bilateral visit.

The Indian government had formally invited Tarique Rahman for a bilateral visit soon after he became prime minister. Later, he was invited to the BRICS outreach session in his capacity as BIMSTEC chair.

While discussions between the two countries over the bilateral visit were under way, the situation became complicated over former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who is currently in India.

Her “continued political campaigning” on Bangladesh while staying in India has cast uncertainty over Tarique Rahman’s visit. As a result, even one week before the BRICS Summit, uncertainty remains over who will represent Bangladesh.

Jaiswal’s response also did not make clear whether someone else would represent Bangladesh if Tarique Rahman does not attend.

It has been alleged that Sheikh Hasina was conducting “anti-state and anti-government campaigning” through her virtual participation in a press conference organised at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club (FCC) in New Delhi on 5 August.

The incident angered the Bangladesh government, which expressed its displeasure in various ways. Dhaka also renewed its demand for Hasina’s extradition and urged the Indian government to restrain her political activities.

The decision not to have Tarique Rahman visit India for a bilateral engagement ahead of the BRICS Summit is linked to the episode.

Following 5 August, Delhi Police recently refused permission for another international discussion in which several people associated with the Awami League, whose activities are banned in Bangladesh, were scheduled to participate.

Hasina has also recently given fresh interviews to several Indian media outlets. The Indian government declined to comment on those interviews on Friday.

Responding to several questions on the matter during the foreign ministry briefing, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the government had nothing to say about it.

A journalist asked whether the timing of Hasina’s interviews was “quite interesting” and whether the Indian government had anything to say about it. Jaiswal replied that he had no comment.

Another journalist said Hasina had told the media outlets that she had no understanding with the Bangladesh government regarding her return to the country in December this year and that no back-channel discussions were taking place with the government.

The journalist said Hasina had sought assurances of personal security in connection with her return, as well as guarantees that she would be able to communicate with her lawyers. She had also said she wanted to ensure a free and impartial trial.

Asked whether Sheikh Hasina had conveyed any of these matters to the Indian government, Jaiswal said he had no information on the issue.

item.title: Raihan posts pistol-firing video hours after Jubo Dal activist shot dead in Raozan
item.description:
Around five and a half hours after a Jubo Dal activist was shot to death in broad daylight in Raozan, Chattogram, Md Raihan posted a video of himself firing a pistol on his Facebook Story. The video was posted at around 3:00 am early Friday.

Raihan is known as an associate of Sazzad Ali alias Boro Sazzad, who is currently absconding abroad.

The video shows Raihan holding a 9mm pistol and firing three shots in succession. However, it could not immediately be confirmed when or where the video was recorded.

Md Russell, additional superintendent of police (media) for Chattogram district, told Prothom Alo, “We are investigating to determine whether it is an old video or one recorded recently.”

According to police and local sources, 35-year-old Raihan studied up to Class-III. He once worked as a CNG-run auto-rickshaw driver. Police allege that he also sold illicit liquor while operating under an assumed identity.

According to the police, Raihan became acquainted with Sazzad Hossain, also known as Chhoto Sazzad, while they were both in prison in connection with an attempted murder case. After securing bail following 5 August 2024, he allegedly became involved in various criminal activities. He has also been accused of firing his weapon indiscriminately.

Police claim that although (Chhoto) Sazzad was recently sent to jail, Raihan is now overseeing his weapons cache.

Police arrested another member of Sazzad Ali’s group, Mobarak Hossain Emon, alias David Emon, in a raid in Jashore on the night of 29 July. On the same day, police conducted an operation in Noakhali to arrest Raihan, but he managed to evade them, according to police.

At around 9:30 pm on Thursday, Jubo Dal activist Muhammad Karim, 35, was shot to death in the Keranihat area of Urkirchar union in Raozan upazila.

According to witnesses, a group of men on four or five motorcycles surrounded Karim after he entered the market. One of them attacked him on the neck and head with a kirich, a traditional curved blade. After Karim fell to the ground, bleeding heavily, several of the attackers shot him. They then fled the scene on motorcycles.

Police said Karim had at least 10 cases filed against him over allegations including theft, drug offences, robbery, mugging and abduction. He had also been imprisoned several times.

item.title: Perception of viewing Hindus as vote bank has shattered: Home Minister
item.description:
The perception of viewing the Hindus as the vote bank of fascist forces has been shattered, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Friday.

He also said the country’s Hindu community had shattered in the 13th parliamentary election the misconception and myth that the fascist forces of the past considered them their vote bank.

The Home Minister made the remarks as the chief guest at a rally held on Friday afternoon before the Janmashtami procession. The rally was held at Palashi intersection in the capital.

After the rally, a procession began from Palashi intersection towards Victoria Park in Old Dhaka.

Speaking about voting in the 13th parliamentary election and helping the BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) win, the Home Minister said, “We believe you have made your judgment. In the last election, you voted against the forces of evil. You will have a role in strengthening democracy and maintaining secularism in the future as well.”

The Home Minister also remarked that in the six months since the government took office, religious practices and religious freedom for people of all faiths have been ensured, which is visible.

Home Minister Salahuddin AhmedAs free citizens of Bangladesh, none of you should identify yourselves as minorities. We hope that none of you will identify yourselves on the basis of religion; identify yourselves on the basis of citizenship.

“The Constitution of Bangladesh assigns the state the responsibility of ensuring the religious freedom to practise all religions, and the state will ensure it. It also says that there can be no discrimination on the basis of religion, and that the freedom of places of worship for followers of all religions and the freedom of those in charge of such places to establish places of worship have been ensured for religious freedom,” he added.

Commenting that it would have been better not to use the word ‘communal’ while talking about maintaining harmony, the Home Minister said, “We use the term communal harmony in a grammatical sense. This is because this term has become established in literature as something that must be maintained. It would have been better if we did not use the word communal. If we had said we would maintain social and religious harmony.”

“From today, we will say that we will maintain religious harmony. We will maintain social harmony and peace. No one needs to mention the term communal harmony anymore. It will be religious harmony, coexistence, and social peace and harmony. We will maintain harmony,” he stated.

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed also urged citizens not to identify themselves as minorities anymore as free citizens of Bangladesh.

He said, “As free citizens of Bangladesh, none of you should identify yourselves as minorities. We hope that none of you will identify yourselves on the basis of religion; identify yourselves on the basis of citizenship.”

The rally, chaired by Gopal Chandra Debnath of the Mahanagar Sarbojanin Puja Committee, was also addressed by Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Hindu, Buddhist, Christian and Ethnic Minority Affairs Bijon Kanti Sarker, Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Abdus Salam, Dhaka-7 MP Hamidur Rahman, Hindu Religious Welfare Trust Vice-Chairman Tapan Chandra Majumdar and senior lawyer Subrata Chowdhury, among others.

item.title: Carry out your long march, but offer an alternative for gas, power
item.description:
Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) Acting Secretary General and Political Adviser to the Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi has called upon the Opposition not to threaten street protests over the gas and electricity crisis, but to present alternative plans and recommendations in Parliament on how the shortages can be addressed.

He said the country’s gas and electricity crisis had been caused by the US-Iran war and the previous government’s flawed planning.

Rizvi made the remarks as the chief guest at the induction ceremony of the newly elected executive committee of the Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association, held at the Jatiya Natyashala Auditorium (national theatre hall) of Shilpakala Academy in Dhaka on Friday afternoon.

“You can hold a long march or announce programmes over gas and electricity—that is fine. But tell us an alternative: how are we going to supply gas and electricity? Where will we get them from, and how will we get them?” Rizvi said.

He further said the Opposition should present a plan outlining what steps should be taken to tackle the current crisis. According to him, Opposition MPs have the opportunity to speak in Parliament.

While criticising the government and holding programmes outside Parliament are normal practices in a democracy, he said, the Opposition should also offer constructive recommendations for addressing the crisis.

The Prime Minister’s political adviser further said, “I do not think it would be right to deliberately create a planned paralysis. Rather, a plan must be put forward on how this crisis can be brought to an end.”

He also warned that if the activities of the past were repeated, the country would be pushed further into darkness.

Pointing to global conflicts and disruptions to the energy supply chain as factors behind the current gas and electricity crisis, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said difficulties had arisen in importing the fuel needed because the transportation of energy through the Strait of Hormuz had been disrupted.

NCP steps up street protests alongside parliament, long marches and mass rally ahead

He claimed that the crisis had not been caused by any action of the government itself.

Rizvi also highlighted the role of songs and dance during the July uprising. He said cultural performances had inspired and emboldened protesters during the movement.

The event was chaired by Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association President Farhana Baby.

State Minister for Road Transport and Railways Habib Ur Rashid Habib, BNP Cultural Affairs Secretary Ashraf Uddin Ujjal, poet Rezauddin Stalin, actor Helal Khan and Zakir Hossain Rukon, among others, attended as special guests.

The newly elected executive committee members of the Bangladesh Dance Artistes Association were later formally inducted.

‘Country will fall behind without equal participation of boys and girls’

Speaking at another programme, BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said the country and society will fall behind unless boys and girls were ensured equal participation in every field, including sports.

He made the remarks as the chief guest at the inaugural ceremony of an inter-divisional Under-16 girls’ football competition organised by the Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association this morning.

Rizvi said, “We know that there are many barriers in our society. But if we are to keep pace with the progress of the world, our girls must come forward, particularly in the field of sports. If we can produce a great athlete among our girls, it will hold our heads high in the eyes of the world. It will also inspire women in other sectors.”

Jamaat warns govt of public backlash if Opposition long march is obstructed

The BNP acting secretary general further said men and women must move forward on an equal footing in every field. Otherwise, he said, the country would fall behind.

“Our Prime Minister has strongly recognised this issue. That is why he has introduced the Notun Kuri Sports programme. Those who are deserving must be given due recognition. Competitions of this kind should be organised in every metropolitan area and district,” he stated.

The Prime Minister’s political adviser also said efforts were under way to establish a sports university in Bangladesh.

In her welcome address, Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association President Sarwat Siraj said there was no alternative to women’s participation in sports if Bangladesh’s nationalist forces were to move forward against “extreme conservatism, religious fanaticism and forces selling tickets to heaven”.

She said the Bangladesh Women’s Sports Association was working towards this goal.

item.title: Prairies, parks, and padfoots: My summer with Canada Geese
item.description:
Coming this far into the Prairies to attend a scientific conference was quite an undertaking, but getting to admire the beauty of Canada Geese each morning near my hotel was deeply rewarding. I could not have asked for anything more precious.
During a two-week stay at a downtown Saskatoon hotel in the summer of 2019, it became a daily routine to encounter gaggles of geese foraging along the South Saskatchewan River. The more I watched them, the more captivated I became by their distinct features. These birds are abundant throughout Saskatoon, particularly along the Meewasin Valley Trail.
Canada Geese grazing near South Saskatchewan River in Saskatoon. Native to North America, these large waterfowl are easily recognized by their long black necks, black heads, and striking white `chinstrap` facial patches. Highly adaptable, they frequently forage on manicured lawns in urban parks. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Throughout the day, I frequently crossed paths with flocks on the grassy waterfront stretches of Kiwanis Park, the manicured lawns of Spadina Crescent East, and in the river itself. As I walked beneath the mature ash and elm canopy along the paved trails flanking the west bank, seeing these geese became a constant and comforting sight.
For about two weeks, I stayed at Delta Hotels Saskatoon Downtown on Twentieth Street East, nestled in Saskatoon’s central business district near the scenic river pathways. The 18-storey structure, originally built in 1983 as the Ramada Renaissance Hotel, is one of the tallest buildings in Saskatoon. It was later renamed the Radisson Hotel Saskatoon before undergoing its most recent transformation. In January 2019, just six months before my visit, the property was rebranded under Marriott International’s Delta Hotels banner.
Two Canada Geese standing on a grassy stretch next to a gravel path along the waterfront at Kiwanis Memorial Park. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
As a guest in Room 619, I frequently encountered Canada Geese in the immediate vicinity of the hotel. Staying just 650 metres from Kiwanis Memorial Park and the sprawling waterfront lawns along the South Saskatchewan River, I was virtually guaranteed to cross paths with them every day.
Located practically across the street and stretching within a few short blocks of the hotel, the beautifully manicured green space of Kiwanis Park on the river’s west bank serves as a primary foraging ground, where gaggles of geese graze on open lawns throughout the day.
The iconic urban canopy of American elm trees shading the brick-paved promenade along Spadina Crescent East. This vibrant Saskatoon riverfront stretch runs right next to Kiwanis Memorial Park, sloping down toward the South Saskatchewan River on the left and the downtown street on the right. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Furthermore, the paved Meewasin Valley Trail runs directly along the riverbank, just steps from the hotel lobby. Along nearby Spadina Crescent East, the geese routinely moved between the river and urban park lawns, occasionally halting downtown traffic as they crossed the busy street.
While Canada Geese have earned a notorious reputation for being cantankerous, fiercely territorial, and hostile towards humans, I pleasantly discovered that this downtown Saskatoon flock was highly urbanized and remarkably calm. They comfortably foraged beside the paved walking paths, paying little attention to me as I photographed them.
A flock of six geese grazing on the riverside lawns of Kiwanis Memorial Park, right besides a winding, paved pedestrian pathway. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
One afternoon, I spotted a few goslings along a stretch of the South Saskatchewan River shoreline, though I missed the opportunity to take a photo. Because it was already late July, I had also missed the chance to witness the local “crèches” by about a month. Had my visit taken place between May and June, I would have had a much better chance of seeing these massive gosling broods along the Meewasin Trail.
During those spring months, dominant adult pairs frequently form cooperative daycares, herding groups of up to 60 fuzzy goslings along pathways and across local streets.
A pair of Canada Geese by the water`s edge, surrounded by tall, dry grasses and reeds. One stands alert while the other rests on the bank, casting a sharp reflection in the calm water. This quiet marshland represents their traditional nesting and foraging habitat. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Had I been in the Canadian Prairies a couple of months earlier, I probably would have witnessed many more goslings than I actually did. Goslings typically hatch in May, resulting in crowded and highly active family scenes along the riverbanks. By mid-summer, geese undergo their annual moult and temporarily lose their flight feathers, meaning they spend considerable time walking around public parks and paths rather than flying.
One afternoon, while sitting on a park bench, I watched a flock of geese frolicking and noticed the distinct physical features that set them apart from other birds. They have solid black heads and long, elegant black necks. Their signature bright white “chinstrap” is impossible to miss — a stark patch running across the throat and up the sides of the face. Their breasts range from light brown to grayish, contrasting beautifully with the scalloped, tan-edged feathers along their backs and wings. Completing their striking appearance, their large webbed feet are deep dark grey or black.
Goslings swimming between two adult Canada Geese. Such large group is known as a crèche. Canada geese frequently combine their goslings into a single “nursery” guarded by a few adult `babysitters`. Cooperative parenting behavior distributes the heavy duty of predator surveillance across fewer adults, dramatically increasing the survival rate of the young goslings. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
That summer 2019 visit to the Canadian Prairies also took me to Alberta. On a road trip from Saskatoon to Edmonton, it drizzled almost the entire way. As I travelled along the Yellowhead Highway (Highway 16), which cuts through the agricultural aspen parkland and prairie regions, I spotted gaggles of geese around many canola fields and prairie sloughs — shallow, swampy wetlands.
Once I reached Edmonton, however, my busy schedule with other commitments did not allow me to visit some of the urban green spaces where I could probably have seen larger goose broods.
Five Canada Geese lined up along the grassy banks of the South Saskatchewan River. Photo: Collected/Dhaka Tribune
Both Saskatchewan and Alberta lie within the “Prairie Pothole Region” and the “Mississippi-Central Flyways”, making them home to some of the highest concentrations of Canada Geese in North America. The regions serve as major migratory hubs as well as permanent breeding grounds.
After reading some literature on geese, I learned that the Canada Goose is widely considered one of the ultimate wildlife conservation success stories, having recovered from near extinction in the early 20th century to a thriving population of millions across North America today.
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, unchecked hunting, habitat loss, and the widespread use of geese as live hunting decoys decimated their populations. Backed by protective measures such as the Migratory Birds Convention Act, aggressive captive-breeding programs and the release of former live decoys helped restore the species across the continent.
Humans also altered the North American landscape in ways that have favoured the survival traits of the Canada Goose. Freshly mowed suburban lawns, corporate parks, golf courses, and agricultural fields now provide prime, nutrient-rich grazing grounds. Human development has also eliminated many major natural predators, removing one of the primary threats to adult geese.
Consequently, many urban goose populations have lost their migratory instincts entirely. Because urban retention ponds and parks rarely freeze completely, millions of geese remain year-round residents of cities.
